The eval layer I'd use is **`@mastra/evals`**. You already run `@mastra/core` 1.79, and its `createScorer` lets one scorer mix code-based and LLM-judge steps, so the deterministic checks you already have become steps inside it rather than getting replaced.

## ⚠️ Your numbers don't match mine
- I couldn't find 67/68 anywhere in the repo.
- `run12-hosted-26b.json` scores 63/64 fields with 0 extra people.
- `pipeline-1.json` also reads 63/64. Its research stage found 17 candidates: 2 high confidence and 15 low.
- So inscription reading isn't where the false positives are. They're in **identity matching** (wrong person accepted) and **story grounding**.

## 🔧 Why `@mastra/evals`
- **Extends what you have:** `createScorer` runs in steps (`preprocess`, then `analyze`, then `generateScore`, then `generateReason`), and each step can be a plain function or a judge prompt.
  - `preprocess` can call your own `verifyFacts` and `groundParagraph` from `src/lib/server/narrative.ts`. Your deterministic layer becomes the first gate and doesn't need rewriting.
- **Prebuilt scorers that fit:**
  - [Faithfulness](https://mastra.ai/reference/evals/faithfulness.md) splits the output into claims and checks each against the context (supported / unsupported / unsure). This directly catches otherworld text stating life facts.
  - [Hallucination](https://mastra.ai/reference/evals/hallucination.md) looks for contradictions and unsupported claims. Its `getContext` hook can feed it the source pages for each run.
- **No cost to generation speed:** the scorers run only in `benchmarks/`, never in the request path. Don't attach them to the live agent, because live scoring adds model calls.
- **Install check:**
  - The latest stable is 1.10.9. Your `@mastra/core` 1.79 is inside its supported range.
  - Its `vitest` peer is `<5`, but it's marked optional, so your vitest 5.0.5 gets no warning as long as you don't use its vitest helpers.
  - It shipped 2026-10-28. If pnpm's release-age check rejects it, pin the previous version (no exclusions, per your rules).

## Eval set I'd build (strict means binary pass/fail per fixture)
| Scorer | Kind | Fails when |
|---|---|---|
| `identity-precision` | code | A low-confidence candidate gets told as that person. A namesake trap fixture resolves to anyone. |
| `fact-isolation` | code, then judge | A sentence in the otherworld/framing text states a date, place, relation or occupation. |
| `faithfulness` | prebuilt judge | Any story claim is unsupported (threshold 1.0, not an average). |
| `insufficient-correct` | code | The story is told when it should have been refused, or the reverse. |

- **Judge model:** Gemini free tier only (per your standing constraint). At 21 fixtures, the rate limits are fine.
- **Ground truth:** the identity and story checks need a `expectedIdentity` label per fixture (person, `none`, or `namesake`). Today's manifest only labels the stone.

## Alternatives I'd skip
- **Evalite:** built on Vitest and nice to use, but its 1.0 has been in beta since Nov 2025 with breaking changes promised ([GitHub](https://github.com/mattpocock/evalite), [v1 docs](https://v1.evalite.dev/)). It would be a new framework for no gain over Mastra.
- **Promptfoo / Braintrust autoevals:** a second eval system next to the Mastra stack you already have. That's YAGNI.

## ❓ One decision before I build
What counts as a false positive for you?
- **(a)** A story told about the wrong person: an identity match. This is where your low-confidence numbers point.
- **(b)** A true person, but the story asserts unsupported facts.

If it's (a), the main fix is likely a gate in `identity.ts`, and evals only measure it. If it's (b), the main fix is the prompt plus `groundParagraph`. Either way, the fixture manifest needs the new identity labels, which you'll have to review.

Snapshot verified 2026-09-04 against <https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/models>. Gemini API
names churn fast — `gemini-3.5-flash` went from default workhorse to legacy baseline in one
quarter. Re-check the docs before writing a model string, and always when the current date is
more than ~3 months past the date above.

## Models

### Text and multimodal (GA)

| API name | Tier | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `gemini-3.8-flash` | Flash | **Default workhorse.** Most intelligent Flash; software engineering and agents. |
| `gemini-3.7-flash` | Flash | Previous generation. Complex coding. Prefer 3.8 for new work. |
| `gemini-3.6-flash` | Flash | Balanced speed and multimodal. |
| `gemini-3.5-flash` | Flash | **Legacy baseline.** High-throughput only. Do not start here. |
| `gemini-3.5-flash-lite` | Flash-Lite | **Fastest and cheapest.** Narrow classification, boolean extraction. |
| `gemini-3.1-flash-lite` | Flash-Lite | Frontier performance at lower cost. |
| `gemini-2.5-pro` | Pro | Hardest multi-step reasoning where accuracy outweighs latency and cost. |
| `gemini-2.5-flash` / `gemini-2.5-flash-lite` | 2.5 | Older line. New work belongs on 3.x. |

### Preview — text and agentic

| API name | Use it for |
|---|---|
| `gemini-3.1-pro-preview` | Advanced intelligence and reasoning. Pro tier — slower and pricier than Flash; justify it on the critical path. |
| `gemini-3-flash-preview` | Frontier performance tier. |

### Audio and speech

| API name | Status | API | Use it for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gemini-3.5-transcribe` | GA | `generateContent` | Speech-to-text with diarization. Batch. |
| `gemini-3.5-transcribe-live` | GA | Live | Streaming speech-to-text. |
| `gemini-3.1-flash-tts-preview` | Preview | `generateContent` | Low-latency TTS with expressive control. |
| `gemini-2.5-flash-preview-tts` | Preview | `generateContent` | Controllable TTS. |
| `gemini-2.5-pro-preview-tts` | Preview | `generateContent` | High-fidelity synthesis — podcasts, audiobooks. |
| `gemini-3.1-flash-live-preview` | Preview | **Live only** | Low-latency audio-to-audio dialogue. |
| `gemini-3.5-live-translate-preview` | Preview | **Live only** | Real-time speech-to-speech translation, 70+ languages. |
| `gemini-2.5-flash-native-audio-preview-12-2025` | Preview | **Live only** | Real-time conversational agents. |

**Check the API column before you pick.** Models marked *Live only* run over the Live API's
stateful WebSocket session. They do **not** work with `generateContent` or `batchGenerateContent`,
and they are speech-**to-speech**: audio in, audio out. They cannot serve an asynchronous
request/response pipeline, and they cannot return structured text. Reaching for one in a batch
job is a rewrite, not a config change.

`gemini-3.5-live-translate-preview` is the most common mistake here — the name reads like a
translation model you could call per request. It is a real-time conversation model built on
Gemini 3 Pro. For translating recorded audio in a batch pipeline, use a normal Flash tier with a
translation instruction and a `responseSchema`.

**Every TTS model is preview.** There is no GA text-to-speech id. Anything shipping TTS carries
preview risk — say so rather than implying stability.

- **Video**: `gemini-omni-1.1-flash` (GA) · `veo-3.1-generate-preview` ·

- **Music**: `lyria-3.5` · `lyria-3-clip-preview` · `lyria-3-pro-preview` · `lyria-realtime-exp`
- **Agents (preview)**: `gemini-2.5-computer-use-preview-10-2025` ·
  `deep-research-preview-04-2026` · `deep-research-max-preview-04-2026` ·
  `antigravity-preview-05-2026` · `gemini-robotics-er-2-preview` ·
  `gemini-robotics-er-1.6-preview`

### Never use — shut down or deprecated

`gemini-2.0-flash` · `gemini-2.0-flash-lite` · `gemini-3.1-flash-lite-preview` ·
`gemini-3-pro-preview` · `imagen-4.0-generate`

### SDK

- **`@google/genai` v2.0.0+**. Pin v2+; the Interactions API broke at v2. Latest 2.21.0.
- `ai.models.generateContent({ model, contents, config })`
- Construct the client server-side only. An API key in browser-reachable code is a leaked key.
- Flash supports Search grounding, Maps grounding, File Search, Code Execution, URL Context,
  and standard function calling.

## Tier selection

Two capability levers: **model** and **thinking level**. Pull both deliberately.

- Smarter (harder reasoning, more reliable tool use) → higher tier and/or higher thinking.
- **Split a multi-call pipeline by job.** Narrow boolean classification belongs on Flash-Lite;
  the one call doing real extraction or transformation belongs on `gemini-3.8-flash`. Running
  every call at the top tier buys latency and cost, not accuracy.
- **Less** optimal (sub-optimal persona, "play like a beginner", looser output) → Flash-Lite
  and/or `MINIMAL` thinking. A bigger model optimizes *harder*; reaching for Pro to make
  something play dumber moves the wrong way. The prompt (negative constraints + few-shot) is
  the primary lever; the smaller tier reinforces it.

## Prompting Flash

Flash 3.5 favors directness over verbosity, logic over persuasion. The prompt is a control
surface, not a conversation. Chain-of-thought prose in the prompt hurts — move reasoning to
the thinking level.

**Structure**

- XML tags **or** markdown headers, never both — mixing muddies the instruction/data boundary.
- Order: `role → instructions → constraints → output`.
- Role + behavioral constraints go in `systemInstruction`. It persists across turns, so each
  user turn carries only the immediate task.
- Data first, task/question **last**. Bridge with "Based on the information above, …".

**Negative constraints** — state them explicitly, placed next to the instruction they guard,
not in a far-off rules dump. Plain and direct ("Do NOT reach for the most-efficient question")
beats hedging.

**Few-shot** — 2–3 examples are the strongest lever for style, persona, and format; stronger
than describing the behavior in prose. Match example complexity to the real task. For a
persona, *show* one turn of it.

**Thinking level** — set `thinkingConfig: { thinkingLevel }`, never "think step by step" in
the prompt.

- `MINIMAL` — fast; also stops a capable model from over-reasoning into behavior you did not
  want (optimal play when you asked for casual).
- `MEDIUM` / `HIGH` — genuine multi-step reasoning where accuracy beats speed.

Replacing verbose CoT prompting with a raised thinking level is a strict improvement. Delete
the CoT.

**Temperature** — 1.0 default. Lower only for deterministic extraction/classification.

**Structured output** — anything beyond trivial JSON gets a `responseSchema` (types, `enum`,
`propertyOrdering`) plus `responseMimeType: 'application/json'`. The schema enforces shape, so
stop babysitting it in prose. Still re-validate the parsed object in code: schema-valid and
semantically wrong is reachable, and a model response is untrusted input.

```
<role>You are [persona] doing [task]. [One line on how it reasons.]</role>

<how_you_work>
- [Imperative steps, one trait/action each.]
</how_you_work>

<never>
- [Explicit negative constraints, each next to the behavior it guards.]
</never>

<examples>
- [1–3 short worked examples that show the desired behavior/persona/format.]
</examples>

<output>[What to return; pair with a responseSchema for JSON.]</output>
```

content.text:
The story eval is wired up on branch `feat/story-evals` and runs with `pnpm eval` (or `make eval`). Baseline: **12 of 21 stories pass** (13 on the first run), so the eval is finding real problems. `make ai-checks` passes; nothing is committed and nothing is pushed.

## 🔧 What changed
- **`benchmarks/evals/life-claims.ts`** — a Mastra `createScorer` built on `@mastra/core`, so no new dependency.
  - A `gemini-3.8-flash` judge (free key, temperature 0) splits each story into claims, marks each as about the person's life or as ghost atmosphere, and quotes the evidence for life claims.
  - Code then confirms each quote appears word for word in the records. The judge can't vouch for words that aren't there.
- **`benchmarks/evals/stone-years.ts`** — a code-only check: every year in the story must fall between the stone's birth and death.
- **`benchmarks/evals/story.eval.ts`** — one test per person.
  - Only the model calls are live; page fetches replay the recorded fixtures.
  - Each test fails if the story is empty, has a year outside the stone's dates, or has any unsupported life claim. It also prints the median story time.
- **`benchmarks/record-stories.ts`** — saves each fixture's search candidates and source page text to `fixtures/stories.json`.
- **`vite.config.ts`** — split into `unit` and `eval` projects. `pnpm test` runs `unit` only, so live calls never reach CI.
- **`package.json`, `Makefile`** — added the `eval` script and target.
- **`src/lib/server/pages.ts`** — fixed a crash in fetching source pages, found while recording.
  - Some sites return a bot wall whose top-level element is a `<script>`, and the page parser (Readability) threw on it, which crashed the whole story request.
  - It now returns `null` like any other unreadable page. The new test fails without the fix.
- **`fixtures/stories.json`** — 21 recorded cases.

## 📊 What the baseline found
- **Ghost lines making claims about the person's life** (what you asked about):
  - "a long life" for a man who died at 45
  - "died too soon", "a life spent in service", "these were the places I called home"
  - "I left pieces of myself behind", "my life was maps and layers"
- **Stories about the wrong person**:
  - Dixon: a namesake born 1914 who died 2021, against a stone that says 1943–2018.
  - Hayden: a vampire from a Twilight fan wiki.
  - Charles Holmquist: an obituary for *Gary* Ray Holmquist, including "died on a Tuesday".
  - Cunningham: an admiral. Doran: a university researcher. Mills: an 85-year-old plus a staff sergeant.
  - The judge already rejects claims when the records clearly describe someone else, so this scorer catches some of the wrong-person problem too.
- **Speed:** stories take a median of 7.5 s. The eval never runs in the request path, so it adds nothing to generation time.

## 🏷️ Labels for you to review
- Every case in `fixtures/stories.json` has `"match": null, "reviewed": false`.
- Set `match` to `0` if the top candidate is the person on the stone, or `-1` if it's someone else.
- `-1` makes the eval use the stone-only story, the same fallback the app uses.
- Each recorded person has at most one candidate, so the only values you'll need are `0` and `-1`.
- From the year mismatches above, I'd set **-1** for Dixon, Hayden, Charles Holmquist, Cunningham and Doran. I haven't looked into the rest.
- These labels are also the ground truth for (a), replacing your manual confirmation step.

## ⚠️ One problem before tuning
- The story model runs at temperature 1, so each run fails a different set: 4 cases failed only in run 1 and 5 only in run 2.
- One sample per case can't tell whether a prompt change helped or just got lucky.
- I recommend 3 samples per case, passing only if all 3 pass. That's about 3× the free-tier calls, around 20 minutes per run.

# Eval-Driven Development for Python LLM Applications

You're building an **automated evaluation pipeline** that tests a Python-based AI application end-to-end — running it the same way a real user would, with real inputs — then scoring the outputs using evaluators and producing pass/fail results via `pixie test`.

**What you're testing is the app itself** — its request handling, context assembly (how it gathers data, builds prompts, manages conversation state), routing, and response formatting. The app uses an LLM, which makes outputs non-deterministic — that's why you use evaluators (LLM-as-judge, similarity scores) instead of `assertEqual` — but the thing under test is the app's code, not the LLM.

During evaluation, the app's own code runs for real — routing, prompt assembly, LLM calls, response formatting — nothing is mocked or stubbed. But the data the app reads from external sources (databases, caches, third-party APIs, voice streams) is replaced with test-specified values via instrumentations. This means each test case controls exactly what data the app sees, while still exercising the full application code path.

**Rule: The app's LLM calls must go to a real LLM.** Do not replace, mock, stub, or intercept the LLM with a fake implementation. The LLM is the core value-generating component — replacing it makes the eval tautological (you control both inputs and outputs, so scores are meaningless). If the project's test suite contains LLM mocking patterns, those are for the project's own unit tests — do NOT adopt them for the eval Runnable.

**The deliverable is a working `pixie test` run with real scores** — not a plan, not just instrumentation, not just a dataset.

This skill is about doing the work, not describing it. Read code, edit files, run commands, produce a working pipeline.

---

## Before you start

**First, activate the virtual environment**. Identify the correct virtual environment for the project and activate it. After the virtual environment is active, run the setup.sh included in the skill's resources.
The script updates the `eval-driven-dev` skill and `pixie-qa` python package to latest version, initialize the pixie working directory if it's not already initialized, and start a web server in the background to show user updates.

**Setup error handling — what you can skip vs. what must succeed:**

- **Skill update fails** → OK to continue. The existing skill version is sufficient.
- **pixie-qa upgrade fails but was already installed** → OK to continue with the existing version.
- **pixie-qa is NOT installed and installation fails** → **STOP.** Ask the user for help. The workflow cannot proceed without the `pixie` package.
- **`pixie init` fails** → **STOP.** Ask the user for help.
- **`pixie start` (web server) fails** → **STOP.** Ask the user for help. Check `server.log` in the pixie root directory for diagnostics. Common causes: port conflict, missing dependency, slow environment. Do NOT proceed without the web server — the user needs it to see eval results.

## The workflow

Follow Steps 1–6 straight through without stopping. Do not ask the user for confirmation at intermediate steps — verify each step yourself and continue.

**How to work — read this before doing anything else:**

- **One step at a time.** Read only the current step's instructions. Do NOT read Steps 2–6 while working on Step 1.
- **Read references only when a step tells you to.** Each step names a specific reference file. Read it when you reach that step — not before.
- **Create artifacts immediately.** After reading code for a sub-step, write the output file for that sub-step before moving on. Don't accumulate understanding across multiple sub-steps before writing anything.
- **Verify, then move on.** Each step has a checkpoint. Verify it, then proceed to the next step. Don't plan future steps while verifying the current one.

**When to stop and ask for help:**

Some blockers cannot and should not be worked around. When you encounter any of the following, **stop immediately and ask the user for help** — do not attempt workarounds:

- **Application won't run due to missing environment variables or configuration**: The app requires environment variables or configuration that are not set and cannot be inferred. Do NOT work around this by mocking, faking, or replacing application components — the eval must exercise real production code. Ask the user to fix the environment setup.
- **App import failures that indicate a broken project**: If the app's core modules cannot be imported due to missing system dependencies or incompatible Python versions (not just missing pip packages you can install), ask the user to fix the project setup.
- **Ambiguous entry point**: If the app has multiple equally plausible entry points and the project analysis doesn't clarify which one matters most, ask the user which to target.

Blockers you SHOULD resolve yourself (do not ask): missing Python packages (install them), missing `pixie` package (install it), port conflicts (pick a different port), file permission issues (fix them).

**Run Steps 1–6 in sequence.** If the user's prompt makes it clear that earlier steps are already done (e.g., "run the existing tests", "re-run evals"), skip to the appropriate step. When in doubt, start from Step 1.

### Step 1: Understand the app and define eval criteria

**First, check the user's prompt for specific requirements.** Before reading app code, examine what the user asked for:

- **Referenced documents or specs**: Does the prompt mention a file to follow (e.g., "follow the spec in EVAL_SPEC.md", "use the methodology in REQUIREMENTS.md")? - **Specified datasets or data sources**: Does the prompt reference specific data files (e.g., "use questions from eval_inputs/research_questions.json", "use the scenarios in call_scenarios.json")? - **Specified evaluation dimensions**: Does the prompt name specific quality aspects to evaluate (e.g., "evaluate on factuality, completeness, and bias", "test identity verification and tool call correctness")? If so, **every named dimension must have a corresponding evaluator** in your test file.

If the prompt specifies any of the above, they take priority. Read and incorporate them before proceeding.

> **Reference**: Read `references/1-a-project-analysis.md` now.

Before looking at code structure or entry points, understand what this software does in the real world — its purpose, its users, the complexity of real inputs, and where it fails. > **Reference**: Read `references/2a-instrumentation.md` now.

Add `wrap()` calls at the app's data boundaries so the eval harness can inject controlled inputs and capture outputs. This makes the app testable without changing its logic.

#### Sub-step 2b: Implement the Runnable

> **Reference**: Read `references/2b-implement-runnable.md` now.

Write a Runnable class that lets the eval harness invoke the app exactly as a real user would. The Runnable should be simple — it just wires up the app's real entry point to the harness interface. If it's getting complicated, something is wrong.

> **Checkpoint**: `pixie_qa/run_app.py` written. The Runnable calls the app's real entry point with real LLM configuration — no mocking, no faking, no component replacement.

> **Reference**: Read `references/2c-capture-and-verify-trace.md` now.

Run the app through the Runnable and capture a trace. The trace proves instrumentation and the Runnable are working correctly, and provides the data shapes needed for dataset creation in Step 4.

### Step 3: Define evaluators

> **Reference**: Read `references/3-define-evaluators.md` now for the detailed sub-steps.

**Goal**: Turn the qualitative eval criteria from Step 1c into concrete, runnable scoring functions. Each criterion maps to either a built-in evaluator, an **agent evaluator** (the default for any semantic or qualitative criterion), or a manual custom function (only for mechanical/deterministic checks like regex or field existence). The evaluator mapping artifact bridges between criteria and the dataset, ensuring every quality dimension has a scorer. Select evaluators that measure the **hard problems** identified in `pixie_qa/00-project-analysis.md` — not just generic quality dimensions.

> **Checkpoint**: All evaluators implemented. `pixie_qa/03-evaluator-mapping.md` written with criterion-to-evaluator mapping and decision rationale. Do NOT read Step 4 instructions yet.

### Step 4: Build the dataset

> **Reference**: Read `references/4-build-dataset.md` now for the detailed sub-steps.

**Goal**: Create the test scenarios that tie everything together — the runnable (Step 2), the evaluators (Step 3), and the use cases (Step 1c). Do NOT read Step 5 instructions yet.

---

### Step 5: Run `pixie test` and fix mechanical issues

> **Reference**: Read `references/5-run-tests.md` now for the detailed sub-steps.

**Goal**: Execute the full pipeline end-to-end and get it running without mechanical errors. This step is strictly about fixing setup and data issues in the pixie QA components (dataset, runnable, custom evaluators) — NOT about fixing the application itself or evaluating result quality. **Cycle rule for iterative runs**: Every successful `pixie test` invocation creates a concrete `pixie_qa/results/<test_id>` directory and starts a new analysis cycle. > **Reference**: Read `references/6-analyze-outcomes.md` now — it has the complete three-phase analysis process, writing guidelines, and output format requirements.

**Goal**: Analyze `pixie test` results in a structured, data-driven process to produce actionable insights on test case quality, evaluator quality, and application quality. The skill is for Python only (`compatibility: Python 3.10+`, harness `pixie-qa`), so it can't run here without adding a second runtime to a TypeScript repo. Its method is still useful. Here's how it compares to what I built:

## 🔍 Eval-driven-dev vs this branch
| Pixie rule | Here |
|---|---|
| Real LLM, never mocked | ✅ Gemma and the judge are live |
| Swap only external data at the edges (`wrap()`) | ✅ Page fetches are replayed; app code runs for real |
| LLM judge for meaning, code for mechanical checks | ✅ Life-claims judge plus the stone-years check |
| Check the evaluator itself before trusting scores | ✅ Already caught the judge flagging "lived a life" and recalibrated it |
| **Capture traces of in-between steps**, not just the final output | ❌ **Gap.** I only score the final paragraph, so I can't tell whether a bad claim came from the extracted facts, the story model, or text that slipped past grounding. |
| **Written eval criteria and a per-run analysis** with evidence | ❌ **Gap.** Criteria live in my chat messages and test names. |
| **Dataset from real data, not project fixtures**, with at least one case whose outcome is uncertain | ⚠️ Partly conflicts with the hand-written set |

## What I'd take from it
- **Traces:** record the verified facts and the pre-grounding paragraph per sample through Mastra's workflow result, so a failure can be blamed on extraction or on the story model. This is the biggest gain.
- **Criteria doc:** add a short `docs/benchmarks/story-evals.md` covering the criteria, how to run the eval, and what labels mean.
- **Real plus synthetic:** the recorded set is the realism check and the hand-written set is the targeted traps. Pixie would argue for the recorded set alone; I'd keep both, since the traps test failure modes real data hits only by luck.

## What I'd skip

result.output:
# Recommendations from "Demystifying evals for AI agents"

## Grader types
- **Code-based graders** (string match, binary tests, static analysis, tool-call and outcome checks) are fast, cheap, objective, and reproducible. They can be brittle and lack nuance.
- **Model-based graders** (rubrics, natural-language assertions, pairwise comparison, reference-based grading, multi-judge consensus) handle open-ended output, but they are non-deterministic, costlier, and need human calibration.
- **Human graders** (SME review, spot checks, A/B tests, inter-annotator agreement) set the gold standard. They are expensive and slow, so use them to calibrate model graders.
- **Scoring** can be weighted, binary (all graders must pass), or hybrid.
- Prefer deterministic graders where possible, LLM graders where needed, and humans for validation.

## Handling non-determinism
- Run multiple trials per task.
- **pass@k** is the chance of at least one success in k attempts. Use it when one good solution is enough.
- **pass^k** is the chance that all k trials succeed. Use it when consistency matters, such as for customer-facing agents. For example, a 75% per-trial rate over three trials gives about 42% for pass^3.

## Capability vs. regression evals
- Capability evals ask what the agent can do. They should start at a low pass rate to give a "hill to climb."
- Regression evals should stay near 100%. They catch backsliding.
- Once a capability eval reaches high pass rates, move it into the regression suite.

## Building tasks
- Start early. "20-50 simple tasks drawn from real failures is a great start."
- Source tasks from manual pre-release checks, bug trackers, support queues, and user-reported failures. Prioritize by user impact.
- Make tasks unambiguous. Two domain experts should independently reach the same pass/fail verdict.
- Confirm each task is solvable by an agent that follows instructions correctly.
- Write a reference solution for each task to prove it is solvable and that the graders work.
- Treat a 0% pass rate across many trials as a likely broken task, "most often a signal of a broken task, not an incapable agent."
- Balance the sets. Test cases where a behavior should occur and where it should not. One-sided sets produce one-sided optimization, such as an agent that searches for everything.

## Harness and isolation
- The eval agent should behave like the production agent.
- Start each trial from a clean environment. Leftover files, caches, or resource limits create correlated failures that look like agent failures.
- Shared state can inflate scores. One example was an agent reading git history from earlier trials.

## Grader design
- Grade the outcome the agent produced, not the exact path it took. Rigid step-order checks punish valid creativity.
- Use partial credit for multi-part tasks so that partial progress shows up in results.
- Calibrate LLM judges against human experts.
- Give LLM judges an escape option, such as returning "Unknown," to reduce hallucinated grades.
- Use structured rubrics. Grade each dimension with its own isolated LLM judge.
- Once the system is robust, human review can be occasional.
- Make graders resistant to bypasses so the agent must solve the problem rather than exploit a loophole.
- Check for grading bugs. Examples from the article include overly strict numeric matching, ambiguous specs, stochastic tasks that cannot be reproduced, and misconfigured thresholds that penalized correct behavior.

## Reading transcripts
- Read transcripts and grades from many trials. This shows whether the agent made a real mistake or the grader rejected a valid solution.
- "Failures should seem fair": it should be clear what the agent got wrong and why.
- Don't trust scores at face value until you have read some transcripts.

## Saturation and maintenance
- **Eval saturation** happens when an agent passes all solvable tasks. At that point the eval only guards against regressions. Gains can look small even when capability has improved a lot.
- Revise evals when grading is unfair, tasks are ambiguous, valid solutions are penalized, or the harness constrains the model.
- Treat the eval suite as a living artifact with clear ownership. Use a dedicated team for core infrastructure, and let domain experts and product teams contribute tasks.
- Practice eval-driven development: define capabilities with evals before agents can meet them.

## Using evals with other methods
- Combine automated evals (fast iteration, CI/CD), production monitoring (ground truth), A/B tests (user outcomes), user feedback, transcript review, and systematic human studies (calibration).
- No single layer catches every issue, so failures that slip past one layer should be caught by another.

## Common pitfalls
- Overly rigid, step-by-step grading
- One-sided problem sets
- Shared state between trials
- Grading bugs and ambiguous specs
- Saturated suites that give no improvement signal
- Trusting automated scores without reading transcripts
- False confidence when evals don't match real usage

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.


Summary:
## 1. Primary Request and Intent

**Original goal**
- Tune the story model to eliminate false positives.
- Keep the otherworld/ghost story from corrupting facts about a person's life.
- Use strict evals without hurting generation speed.
- Suggest an actual eval library, preferably one that extends existing libs.
- **Decision:** Mastra's `createScorer` from `@mastra/core/evals` (already a dependency), run under Vitest.

**User directives (in order)**
- "the story should always be told."
- (a) Identity: there is currently a human validation step the user wants removed if possible.
- (b) Story-content grounding: the baseline, build it first.
- Create a new branch, wire evals up to run like tests do, and add fixture labels for the user to review.
- Use 3 samples per case, passing only if all pass (pass^3).
- Build both a hand-written fixture set and the recorded SerpApi set ("do both").
- Read and apply ideas from:
  - https://github.com/github/awesome-copilot/blob/main/skills/eval-driven-dev/SKILL.md
  - https://www.anthropic.com/research/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents
- **Critical correction:** true ambience must stay. "If they died at 96 it WAS a long life. That is correct." The rule is that a claim fails only if it is false or invented. Lines implied by the records or the stone's dates pass.
- Add tests confirming gender (narrator voice) picks.
- Start returning the place they lived or died, to improve search guesses.
  - User chose: browser geolocation, plus EXIF GPS fallback for gallery uploads, plus places carved on the stone.
  - Reverse geocoder: Nominatim.
- Latest: "Do the ab benchmark. We do not have quota left to check" (SerpApi quota is nearly exhausted).

## 2. Key Technical Concepts

**Eval design**
- Mastra `createScorer` pipeline: function steps plus LLM-judge prompt-object steps.
- `analyzeStepResult`, `generateScore`, `generateReason`, `scorer.run({input, output})`.
- Judge model: `google/gemini-3.8-flash` (free Gemini key), temperature 0.
- Generator model: `google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it`; story step runs at temperature 1.
- The judge's evidence quotes are verified verbatim in code (normalized substring with record boundaries).
- Judge escape option `unsure`, counted as a failure.
- Reference stories per hand-written case (good must pass, bad must fail) to validate the graders.
- pass@1 vs pass^3 reporting.
- Capability vs regression evals (from the Anthropic article).

**Test harness**
- Vitest `projects`: `unit` and `eval`. `pnpm test` runs `--project unit` only.
- `vi.hoisted` uses `process.getBuiltinModule('node:fs')` because imports aren't available yet.
- `process.loadEnvFile('.env')`.
- `vi.mock('$app/env/private')` and `vi.mock` of `pages.ts` to replay recorded page text.
- `expect.soft`.

**App and pipeline**
- SvelteKit app, Node 26.12.1, pnpm 11.28.9 via Volta (`VOLTA_FEATURE_PNPM=1`), TS strict, ESM.
- Story workflow: `fetchPage` → `extractFacts` → `verifyFacts` → `tellStory` → `groundParagraph`. Falls back to `runStoneStory`.
- `narratorVoice` picks the voice from pronoun cues in fact quotes, then the name guess, then the fallback `female`.

**Place feature**
- `navigator.geolocation` (coarse, 8 s patience).
- `exifreader` 4.52.0, parsing only the Exif block.
- Nominatim reverse geocode:
  - Coordinates rounded to 2 decimals.
  - One request per second, as its policy requires.
  - User-Agent identifies the app.
  - OSM attribution shown in the UI.
- `buildQuery` adds the place unquoted and lowercased, so a carved "OR" can't act as an operator.

**Workflow**
- Git worktree `.worktrees/place` (excluded via `.git/info/exclude`).
- `playwright.config.ts` has `testIgnore: '**/.worktrees/**'`, so e2e needs a temporary config in a worktree.

## 3. Files and Code Sections

### Branch `feat/story-evals` (main checkout `/Users/anchildress1/git_personal/gravespeaker`, uncommitted)

**`src/lib/server/pages.ts`** (bug fix)
- Readability threw on bodies that linkedom parses without an `<html>` root, crashing the story request (e.g. `ru.kinorium.com` bot wall with a `<script>` root).
- Fix:
```ts
const { document } = parseHTML(body);
let text: string | null | undefined;
try {
    text = new Readability(document as unknown as Document).parse()?.textContent;
} catch {
    // Readability throws on documents linkedom builds without an <html> root, such as bot walls.
    return null;
}
return text?.replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim() || null;
```
- `pages.test.ts`: `it.each` test "returns null for an HTML response with %s" covering no markup and a script-only root. Verified failing before the fix.

**`benchmarks/evals/life-claims.ts`** (Mastra scorer)
- `JUDGE_MODEL = 'google/gemini-3.8-flash'`.
- `claimSchema`: `claim`, `kind` (`life` | `atmosphere` | `unsure`), `evidence` (nullable).
- `JUDGE_INSTRUCTIONS`, current text:
  - Splits the story into claims.
  - `life` = about the real person while alive.
  - `atmosphere` = the fictional frame.
  - Otherworld-dressed life details count as `life`.
  - What's true of every dead person (lived, breathed, born, died, time has passed) is `atmosphere`.
  - "How the life or death went is "life", and it holds when the records imply it. Died at 96: "a long life" holds. Died at 19: "gone too soon" holds. An organ donor: "pieces of me live on" holds. Died at 45: "a long life" is false."
  - `unsure` when the judge can't tell; use it instead of guessing.
  - evidence: "copy the exact words from the records that state the claim, or that it follows from directly."
  - never: don't mark a claim `atmosphere` because it's poetic; never give evidence that only makes a claim plausible ("must state the claim or prove it").
- `norm()` removes U+FFFD, lowercases, and collapses non-letters/digits.
- `auditClaims(claims, context)`:
  - Returns `{checked, unsupported}`.
  - `checked` = non-atmosphere claims.
  - `unsupported` = every `unsure` claim, plus claims with missing evidence or evidence not found as ` ${evidence} ` in the records joined by ` | `.
- `lifeClaimsScorer(apiKey)`:
  - `analyze` prompt: `<records>…</records><story subject=…>…</story>` then "Based on the records above, list every claim the story makes."
  - Score = (checked − unsupported) / checked, or 1 when there are none.
  - Reason lists `${kind}: ${claim} (evidence: …)`.

**`benchmarks/evals/life-claims.test.ts`**
- 9 unit tests: supported, case/quote insensitivity, null evidence, evidence absent, partial-word, stitched across records, U+FFFD, unsure fails, atmosphere ignored.

**`benchmarks/evals/stone-years.ts`**
- `yearsOutsideLife(paragraph, inscription, today = new Date())`: 4-digit numbers ≤ the current year that fall outside [born year, died year]. Skips illegible `?` dates and house numbers past the current year.
- `ageAtDeath(inscription)`: "I died at N years old." with full dates (birthday adjusted), "about N" with only years, null otherwise.
- `stone-years.test.ts` covers both.

**`benchmarks/evals/story.eval.ts`**
- Loads `sets = { written: fixtures/stories-written.json, recorded: fixtures/stories-recorded.json }`.
- Mocks `$app/env/private` and `../../src/lib/server/pages.ts` (`fetchPage` replays the recorded pages).
- `SAMPLES = 3`.
- `told(c)`: `match === -1` → stone story; otherwise `candidates[match ?? 0]`.
- `grade(c, paragraph, fromRecords)`: context = epitaph + `ageAtDeath`, plus all candidate source page texts when told from records. Returns `{years, score: result.score ?? 0, reason}`.
- `describe.each(Object.entries(sets))`:
  - Grader test for cases with `good`/`bad` (good must match `{years: [], score: 1}`; bad must score < 1).
  - Per-sample test: story must be non-empty; tracks trials and voices.
  - Soft expects: voice, years, score.
- `afterAll` prints story median ms, per-set voice x/y, pass@1, and pass^3.
- `StoryCase` fields: `inscription`, `candidates`, `pages`, `match`, `reviewed`, `voice`, `good?`, `bad?`.

**`benchmarks/record-stories.ts`**

- Writes `fixtures/stories-recorded.json` with `match: null, reviewed: false, voice: p.voice`.

**`fixtures/manifest.json`**

**`benchmarks/score.ts`**

- New "Voice correct" table row. Run 12 scores 21/21.

**`vite.config.ts`**
```ts
test: {
  expect: { requireAssertions: true },
  environment: 'node',
  projects: [
    { extends: true, test: { name: 'unit', include: ['src/**/*.{test,spec}.ts', 'scripts/**/*.{test,spec}.ts', 'benchmarks/**/*.test.ts'] } },
```

**Recording and grading bugs**
- **`fetchPage` crash on documents without a root element:** the first guard (`!document.documentElement`) wasn't enough because a script root is stripped later. Fixed with try/catch around Readability. Tests fail before the fix.

The commit is the deliverable — no draft file, no push.

## Boundaries

The only repo-mutating commands permitted are `git commit -S` and path-explicit `git add` under
[Staging](#staging). Everything else is off-limits:

| Never | Why |
| - | - |
| Add to a non-empty index | A staged diff is the user's scope decision; commit exactly it |
| `git add -A` / `.` / `-u` / globs | Sweeps unrelated edits into the commit |
| `git push`, `rebase`, `reset`, `commit --amend` | History mutation isn't this skill's job |
| `--no-verify`, `--no-gpg-sign` | Hooks and signing must run |
| Edit source, docs, or config | No formatters, lint fixes, refactors, or test runs |
| Commit on `main`/`master` | Unless the user directed it **this turn** |
| Omit the AI-attribution trailer | A message without it is a failed message |

## Abort conditions

Stop and report; do not work around:

- No staged diff and the request names no work to commit ("commit" alone, tree holds several
  changes) → `nothing staged`; ask which change.
- On `main`/`master` without explicit authorization this turn.
- Diff changed between derivation and commit (see step 5).

## Staging

Only when the index is empty.

- Stage by explicit path every file — tracked and untracked — that belongs to the change the user
  named this turn ("commit the fiji work", "commit this").
- Dirty paths outside that change, or a file mixing it with another concern → stop, list them, ask.
  A pre-commit hook that re-stages fixed files can sweep unstaged edits into the commit.
- Report the staged paths with the SHA.

## Splitting one working tree into atomic commits

Only on an explicit request this turn.

Run steps 1–7 once per group, deriving each message from that group's staged diff alone.

- One logical change per commit. A subject that needs "and" is two commits.
- Every commit stands alone: the tree builds and imports resolve at **each** SHA, not just at the
  tip. Verify before moving to the next group.
- Never hand-split hunks in a file carrying two concerns — that is where work silently disappears.
  Instead: copy the finished files outside the repo, revert the *other* concern out of the file and
  commit, restore the copy and commit the remainder, then diff the tree against the copy. A
  non-empty diff means the split dropped work.
- Report every SHA and subject, not just the last.

## 1. Resolve scope

Precedence, first match wins. Jira key regex `[A-Z][A-Z0-9]+-\d+`, matched case-insensitively,
emitted uppercase:

1. User-provided key (request or `argument-hint`)
2. Branch name — `git --no-pager rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD`
3. None — omit the scope

Never invent a keyword scope (`core`, `api`, `docs`) when no issue key exists. An absent scope is
correct; a made-up one is noise. The diff informs type and subject, never scope.

## 2. Acquire diff

```bash
git --no-pager diff --cached
```

Empty → run [Staging](#staging), then re-run this command. Never derive from `git diff` of the
working tree: `git commit` records the index, so unstaged edits are not in the commit.

Derive everything from hunks only: chat history, prior commits, and memory are not evidence of
what this diff changes.

## 3. Pick type

First match wins:

| Signal | Type |
| - | - |
| Public API removed, signature changed, config key dropped | breaking — add `!` and/or `BREAKING CHANGE:` |
| New user-visible capability | `feat` |
| Defect repair, no new surface | `fix` |
| Faster, same behavior | `perf` |
| Restructure, same behavior | `refactor` |
| Whitespace, formatting, semicolons | `style` |
| Tests only | `test` |
| Docs, comments, JSDoc/KDoc only | `docs` |
| `.github/workflows`, `.circleci`, CI config | `ci` |
| Build system, deps, packaging | `build` |
| Reverts a prior commit | `revert` |
| Maintenance, no production impact | `chore` |

## 4. Pick attribution tier

Exactly one, from diff hunks + this session:

| AI share of the work | Trailer |
| - | - |
| Majority | `Generated-by` |
| Roughly half | `Co-authored-by` |
| Minor assist | `Assisted-by` |
| Only wrote this message | `Commit-generated-by` |

Uncertain → pick the tier that credits the human more.

`Co-authored-by` is the one tier GitHub actually parses and renders on the commit, which is the
point of it — don't substitute a variant spelling. The other three are custom trailers that git
carries verbatim.

## 5. Compose and validate

```
<type>[(<scope>)][!]: <subject>

- <single-line bullet>
- <single-line bullet>

<footers>
```

Format constraints — every one maps to a commitlint rule, so a violation is a hook failure, not a
style opinion:

- Subject ≤ 72 chars, no trailing period, imperative present tense. Not Title Case, sentence-case,
  PascalCase, or UPPER — but real identifiers keep their casing (`OAuth2`, `JSDoc`, `API`)
- Type lowercase, from the enum in step 3
- Body and footer lines ≤ 100 chars; bullets never wrap
- Exactly one blank line after the subject, exactly one before the footers, none elsewhere
- Group changes and say *what* and *why*. File-by-file listings and *how* are wasted lines.
  Quantify where it helps ("add 3 fixtures", "drop 412 LOC").

Footer order, when present:

1. `Refs: PROJ-123` / `Closes #42`
2. `BREAKING CHANGE: <incompatibility and required action>` — only when the `!` alone doesn't
   tell the user what to do. Both forms together are valid.
3. AI attribution — required, exactly one, from step 4.

Trailers use `-` for spaces (`Reviewed-by`); `BREAKING CHANGE` is the spec's one exemption. A
footer too long to fit in 100 chars folds onto a continuation line with a leading space.

**Match the repo before emitting.** Read `commitlint.config.js` (or `.commitlintrc*`) if present

Re-run the step 2 command immediately before committing. If it changed, the message describes

```bash

<full message including blank lines and footers>
EOF
```

`-F -` preserves blank lines and trailers exactly; `-m` with embedded newlines is where formatting
gets mangled. Report the short SHA and subject.
